power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Cognitive decline, cardiometabolic dysfunction, and psychological disorders (particularly late-life depression and anxiety) are highly prevalent in aging, often co-occur, and predict each other over time.

Importantly, stress exposure across the lifespan and dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitaryadrenal (HPA) axis and the autonomic nervous system (ANS), the two main biological stress systems, are considered causes and exacerbators of these age-related conditions.
However, the stress-to-disease pathway in aging has proven hard to demonstrate consistently, and health trajectories vary widely between individuals.

We argue that this partly reflects how the problem has been modeled, with cognitive, cardiometabolic, and psychological health problems in aging studied as separate downstream outcomes of stress and HPA axis and ANS dysregulation.
We review and propose several neurocognitive, neurovisceral, and psychophysiological mechanisms that may explain how these three conditions form a mutually reinforcing system.
Importantly, these mechanisms also feed back onto the HPA axis and ANS, disrupting their circadian and context-sensitive regulation.
We identify middle adulthood as the period in which these reciprocal influences strengthen.
Moreover, we propose that the domain first affected and individual reserve shape the health trajectory and which conditions cooccur.

In this framework, we argue that stress-system dysregulation in aging should be considered both a cause and a consequence of cognitive decline, cardiometabolic dysfunction, depression and anxiety, forming a self-maintaining loop that may provide a systems-level mechanism through which stressrelated multimorbidity contributes to trajectories commonly associated with accelerated biological aging.

Aging is characterized by the convergence of cognitive decline, cardiometabolic dysfunction, and psychological disorders, such as depression and anxiety (Hedden and Gabrieli, 2004; Hirode and Wong, 2020; GBD 2019 Mental Disorders Collaborators, 2022).
text.formatted: Aging is characterized by the convergence of cognitive decline, cardiometabolic dysfunction, and psychological disorders, such as depression and anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(Hedden and Gabrieli, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Hirode and Wong, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">GBD 2019</ref> <ref type="bibr">Mental Disorders Collaborators, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Age-related cognitive change is detectable well before old age, with longitudinal declines in reasoning evident among adults aged 45-49 years and increasing with advancing age (Singh-Manoux et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Age-related cognitive change is detectable well before old age, with longitudinal declines in reasoning evident among adults aged 45-49 years and increasing with advancing age <ref type="bibr" target="#b210">(Singh-Manoux et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Changes in cognition have been most frequently investigated and documented in executive functions, which are cognitive processes supported by the prefrontal cortex (Cabeza and Dennis, 2013), including mental flexibility, inhibitory control, and working memory (Fisk and Sharp, 2004; Hedden and Gabrieli, 2004), but also in episodic memory, which is thought to be partially explained by age-related decline in executive functions (Crawford et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Changes in cognition have been most frequently investigated and documented in executive functions, which are cognitive processes supported by the prefrontal cortex <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Cabeza and Dennis, 2013)</ref>, including mental flexibility, inhibitory control, and working memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Fisk and Sharp, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Hedden and Gabrieli, 2004)</ref>, but also in episodic memory, which is thought to be partially explained by age-related decline in executive functions <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Crawford et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">Lee et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Such agerelated change is not, in itself, a sign of dysfunction, but there is considerable interindividual variability in the timing and magnitude of these changes (Reuter-Lorenz and Park, 2014), with some individuals showing a decline that exceeds what would be expected for a person's age and education (i.e., what we refer to in this review as 'cognitive decline'), even though clinical thresholds are not reached, and such decline may or may not reflect emerging neurodegenerative or cerebrovascular disease (Boyle et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Such agerelated change is not, in itself, a sign of dysfunction, but there is considerable interindividual variability in the timing and magnitude of these changes <ref type="bibr" target="#b189">(Reuter-Lorenz and Park, 2014)</ref>, with some individuals showing a decline that exceeds what would be expected for a person's age and education (i.e., what we refer to in this review as 'cognitive decline'), even though clinical thresholds are not reached, and such decline may or may not reflect emerging neurodegenerative or cerebrovascular disease <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Boyle et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Cardiometabolic burden follows a similarly marked age gradient.

In US population data, metabolic syndrome was present in 39.4% of adults aged 40-59 years and 48.6% of those aged 60 years or older, compared with 19.5% of adults aged 20-39 years (Hirode and Wong, 2020).
text.formatted: In US population data, metabolic syndrome was present in 39.4% of adults aged 40-59 years and 48.6% of those aged 60 years or older, compared with 19.5% of adults aged 20-39 years <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">(Hirode and Wong, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Depression and anxiety, two of the most frequent mental disorders, also remain major sources of disability throughout the second half of life (GBD 2019 Mental Disorders Collaborators, 2022).
text.formatted: Depression and anxiety, two of the most frequent mental disorders, also remain major sources of disability throughout the second half of life <ref type="bibr">(GBD 2019</ref> <ref type="bibr">Mental Disorders Collaborators, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast to age-related cardiometabolic disorders and cognitive decline, which are observed particularly in late adulthood, depression and anxiety are highly prevalent across the lifespan (Kessler et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In contrast to age-related cardiometabolic disorders and cognitive decline, which are observed particularly in late adulthood, depression and anxiety are highly prevalent across the lifespan <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">(Kessler et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">Liu et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, some specific forms of depression and anxiety have been associated with aging.

Late-life depression (LLD) is conventionally defined as a depressive disorder, most often major depressive disorder, but also dysthymia and clinically significant subthreshold syndromes, occurring in adults aged 60 years or older (Butters et al., 2008; Koenig et al., 2014; Teixeira et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Late-life depression (LLD) is conventionally defined as a depressive disorder, most often major depressive disorder, but also dysthymia and clinically significant subthreshold syndromes, occurring in adults aged 60 years or older <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Butters et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">Koenig et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b220">Teixeira et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Approximately 5% of community-dwelling older adults meet full DSM-5 criteria, while a further 10-16% show clinically significant depressive symptoms that do not meet full criteria (for a review, see Szymkowicz et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Approximately 5% of community-dwelling older adults meet full DSM-5 criteria, while a further 10-16% show clinically significant depressive symptoms that do not meet full criteria (for a review, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b218">Szymkowicz et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: LLD comprises early-onset cases (conventionally those with a first episode before age 50-60) that recur or persist into later life, and late-onset cases in which the first lifetime episode appears after that age (Butters et al., 2008; Koenig et al., 2014).
text.formatted: LLD comprises early-onset cases (conventionally those with a first episode before age 50-60) that recur or persist into later life, and late-onset cases in which the first lifetime episode appears after that age <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Butters et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">Koenig et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Compared with depression in younger adults, LLD is less likely to present with prominent sadness and is more likely to show somatic symptoms such as gastrointestinal distress, sleep disorders, or fatigue (Gallo et al., 1997; Hegeman et al., 2012; see also Koenig et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Compared with depression in younger adults, LLD is less likely to present with prominent sadness and is more likely to show somatic symptoms such as gastrointestinal distress, sleep disorders, or fatigue <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Gallo et al., 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Hegeman et al., 2012</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">Koenig et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Late-life anxiety (LLA) has received considerably less attention despite being more frequent than depression, with 12-month prevalence estimates of up to 11.6% and lifetime estimates as high as 15.1% in the United States (Kessler et al., 2005; Reynolds et al., 2015; Ramos and Stanley, 2018) and estimates of 1.2-15% across DSM-5 categories (Hellwig and Domschke, 2019).
text.formatted: Late-life anxiety (LLA) has received considerably less attention despite being more frequent than depression, with 12-month prevalence estimates of up to 11.6% and lifetime estimates as high as 15.1% in the United States <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">(Kessler et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b191">Reynolds et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b185">Ramos and Stanley, 2018)</ref> and estimates of 1.2-15% across DSM-5 categories <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Hellwig and Domschke, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Subthreshold anxiety appears at least as prevalent as anxiety disorders in later life (Witlox et al., 2021), and community estimates of clinically significant anxiety symptoms range from 15% to 52% (Bryant et al., 2008; Yochim et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Subthreshold anxiety appears at least as prevalent as anxiety disorders in later life <ref type="bibr" target="#b247">(Witlox et al., 2021)</ref>, and community estimates of clinically significant anxiety symptoms range from 15% to 52% <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Bryant et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b249">Yochim et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Agoraphobia, panic disorder, and generalized anxiety disorder are the most common in older adults (Hellwig and Domschke, 2019).
text.formatted: Agoraphobia, panic disorder, and generalized anxiety disorder are the most common in older adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Hellwig and Domschke, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Like LLD, LLA appears to follow a bimodal onset distribution, with a substantial group reporting symptoms since late adolescence or early adulthood and another reporting first onset after approximately age 50 (Le Roux et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Like LLD, LLA appears to follow a bimodal onset distribution, with a substantial group reporting symptoms since late adolescence or early adulthood and another reporting first onset after approximately age 50 <ref type="bibr" target="#b111">(Le Roux et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, these conditions do not occur in isolation, as cognitive decline, cardiometabolic dysfunction, depression and anxiety increasingly converge in the second half of life.

In this context, population-based evidence increasingly demonstrates links (in some cases bidirectional) among cognitive, psychological, and metabolic health problems (Pan et al., 2012; Bangen et al., 2019; Firth et al., 2019; Szymkowicz et al., 2023; van Nieuwkerk et al., 2023; Ijaz et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In this context, population-based evidence increasingly demonstrates links (in some cases bidirectional) among cognitive, psychological, and metabolic health problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b165">(Pan et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Bangen et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Firth et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b218">Szymkowicz et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b236">van Nieuwkerk et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Ijaz et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b248">Yang et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b254">Zhang et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These associations are not simply explained by health-risk behavior as a common exposure, as they persist after adjustment for age, sex, education and selected health-related factors (e.g., smoking, physical activity and body mass index), although the covariates considered vary across studies and residual confounding, particularly by broader social determinants, cannot be excluded. (e.g., Batelaan et al., 2016; Schmitz et al., 2018; Firth et al., 2019; Koutsonida et al., 2022) Still, the mechanisms by which these conditions become intertwined and the factors that drive the considerable interindividual variability in their emergence and progression remain poorly understood, limiting our ability to identify at-risk individuals, detect early intervention targets, and develop effective prevention and treatment strategies.

(e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Batelaan et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b203">Schmitz et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Firth et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">Koutsonida et al., 2022)</ref> Still, the mechanisms by which these conditions become intertwined and the factors that drive the considerable interindividual variability in their emergence and progression remain poorly understood, limiting our ability to identify at-risk individuals, detect early intervention targets, and develop effective prevention and treatment strategies.

text.text: Stress and its physiological mediators are considered key drivers and exacerbators of these agerelated health outcomes (Belvederi Murri et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2014; Schlaich et al., 2015; De Looze et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Stress and its physiological mediators are considered key drivers and exacerbators of these agerelated health outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Belvederi Murri et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b119">Liu et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b201">Schlaich et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">De Looze et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and the autonomic nervous system (ANS) coordinate the allocation of physiological resources necessary for adaptive responses to environmental and internal demands (Sapolsky et al., 2000).
text.formatted: The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and the autonomic nervous system (ANS) coordinate the allocation of physiological resources necessary for adaptive responses to environmental and internal demands <ref type="bibr" target="#b199">(Sapolsky et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: The HPA axis exerts many of its effects through glucocorticoid release, whereas the ANS regulates physiological activity through the coordinated action of its sympathetic and parasympathetic branches (Thayer and Lane, 2000; Sapolsky et al., 2000; Ulrich-Lai and Herman, 2009; Russell and Lightman, 2019).
text.formatted: The HPA axis exerts many of its effects through glucocorticoid release, whereas the ANS regulates physiological activity through the coordinated action of its sympathetic and parasympathetic branches <ref type="bibr" target="#b221">(Thayer and Lane, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b199">Sapolsky et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b228">Ulrich-Lai and Herman, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b195">Russell and Lightman, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Sympathetic activation involves the release of catecholamines, particularly adrenaline and noradrenaline (heightening blood pressure, heart rate, and inflammation, among others), while parasympathetic regulation is largely mediated by the vagus nerve, which provides inhibitory control over cardiac and other visceral functions (Sapolsky et al., 2000; Ulrich-Lai and Herman, 2009; Lamotte et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Sympathetic activation involves the release of catecholamines, particularly adrenaline and noradrenaline (heightening blood pressure, heart rate, and inflammation, among others), while parasympathetic regulation is largely mediated by the vagus nerve, which provides inhibitory control over cardiac and other visceral functions <ref type="bibr" target="#b199">(Sapolsky et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b228">Ulrich-Lai and Herman, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b110">Lamotte et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond stress responses, diurnal variation in HPA-axis and ANS functioning also modulates adaptation to the environment (Adam et al., 2017; Hidalgo et al., 2021; Mather, 2024).
text.formatted: Beyond stress responses, diurnal variation in HPA-axis and ANS functioning also modulates adaptation to the environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adam et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Hidalgo et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b130">Mather, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Problems emerge when individuals are exposed to chronic or repeated stressors accumulated across their lifespan (including ongoing psychosocial demands and stressful life events), as such exposure progressively disrupts HPA axis and ANS regulation, leading to less context-sensitive and flexible regulation, which may manifest as elevated or blunted activity, altered circadian organization, exaggerated or insufficient reactivity, and impaired recovery (Gaffey et al., 2016; Pulopulos and Kozusznik, 2018; Thayer et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Problems emerge when individuals are exposed to chronic or repeated stressors accumulated across their lifespan (including ongoing psychosocial demands and stressful life events), as such exposure progressively disrupts HPA axis and ANS regulation, leading to less context-sensitive and flexible regulation, which may manifest as elevated or blunted activity, altered circadian organization, exaggerated or insufficient reactivity, and impaired recovery <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Gaffey et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b175">Pulopulos and Kozusznik, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b223">Thayer et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Dysregulation of these stress-related systems triggers a chain reaction across interconnected biological systems, leading to a collective collapse as individual biomarkers decline and trend toward disease (Juster and Misiak, 2023).
text.formatted: Dysregulation of these stress-related systems triggers a chain reaction across interconnected biological systems, leading to a collective collapse as individual biomarkers decline and trend toward disease <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">(Juster and Misiak, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This cumulative physiological burden has been conceptualized as allostatic load (McEwen and Stellar, 1993; McEwen, 1998; McEwen, 2002; Juster et al., 2010).
text.formatted: This cumulative physiological burden has been conceptualized as allostatic load <ref type="bibr" target="#b137">(McEwen and Stellar, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b133">McEwen, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b134">McEwen, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">Juster et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Within this framework, dysregulation of primary stress systems progressively alters metabolic, cardiovascular, and immune parameters that have shifted but remain subclinical, such as glucose and lipid profiles, insulin sensitivity, visceral adiposity, and blood pressure.

Alterations in these secondary systems, in turn, are held to give rise to tertiary outcomes, that is, cardiometabolic disease, cognitive impairment, psychiatric morbidity, and mortality (Juster et al., 2010; see also McEwen, 2008).
text.formatted: Alterations in these secondary systems, in turn, are held to give rise to tertiary outcomes, that is, cardiometabolic disease, cognitive impairment, psychiatric morbidity, and mortality <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">(Juster et al., 2010</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">McEwen, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, allostatic load overlaps with biological aging, understood as the timedependent decline in physiological integrity that varies among people of the same chronological age (Hastings et al., 2022; Zhang, 2023).

text.text: Higher allostatic load is linked to accelerated biological aging, especially in middle age (Teferi et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026), and cognitive decline, cardiometabolic dysregulation, and late-life depression and anxiety can be conceptualized as conditions characterized by accelerated biological aging (Alexopoulos, 2019; Gonzales et al., 2022; Szymkowicz et al., 2023).

text.text: Empirical evidence and theoretical models from different fields suggest that there are strong mechanistic reasons to consider dysregulation of the HPA axis and the ANS as major contributors to cognitive decline, cardiometabolic dysfunction, depression, and anxiety in middle-aged and older adults (e.g., Baeken and De Raedt, 2011; Belvederi Murri et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2014; Schlaich et al., 2015; Thayer et al., 2021).

text.text: Sustained or poorly regulated HPA axis and ANS activity can influence glucose and lipid metabolism, insulin sensitivity, visceral adiposity, blood pressure, endothelial function, and other processes central to cardiometabolic disease (Schlaich et al., 2015; Ortiz et al., 2022).

text.text: The same biological stress systems have also been linked to structural and functional differences in the brain, including prefrontal and hippocampal circuits critical for executive functions and memory, providing a pathway through which cumulative stress exposure may contribute to cognitive decline (McEwen, 2002; Frewen et al., 2013; Gupta and Morley, 2014; Pulopulos et al., 2014; Pulopulos et al., 2016; Montoliu et al., 2018; Zeki Al Hazzouri et al., 2018).

text.text: Both depression and anxiety are associated with dysregulation (observed in stress-induced responses, circadian activity and resting conditions) in HPA axis and ANS activity in young and older adults (Kemp et al., 2010; Stetler and Miller, 2011; Belvederi Murri et al., 2014; Chalmers et al., 2014; Puig-Perez et al., 2016; Goncharova, 2020; Rashid et al., 2023), and several frameworks have proposed that dysregulation of stress biological systems may lead to the development, maintenance, and recurrence of depression and anxiety via its structural and functional effects on frontolimbic regions involved in emotion and stress regulation (Baeken and De Raedt, 2011; Hellwig and Domschke, 2019; Szymkowicz et al., 2023).

text.text: Thus, the HPA axis and autonomic dysregulation have been conceptualized as mechanistic contributors and candidate causal mediators linking stress exposure throughout the lifespan to cognitive, cardiometabolic, and psychological problems later in life.

However, it is important to note that this apparently straightforward stress-to-disease pathway in aging has proven difficult to demonstrate consistently (e.g., Comijs et al., 2010; Gaysina et al., 2014; Pulopulos et al., 2014; Singh-Manoux et al., 2014; Pulopulos et al., 2016; Christian et al., 2023; Li et al., 2026; Wilson et al., 2024), and a large interindividual variability exists, with older adults showing markedly different physiological profiles and health trajectories (e.g., Puig-Pérez et al., 2015; Puig-Pérez et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2022; Maksyutynska et al., 2024; Wilson et al., 2024).

text.text: Thus, although stress exposure can accelerate cognitive changes and lead to and exacerbate cardiometabolic dysfunction and psychological disorders, the mapping from stress to HPA axis and ANS dysregulation and from this dysregulation to specific health outcomes in aging remains poorly understood.
In this review, we propose that part of this inconsistency may stem from how the problem itself has been modeled.

Cognitive decline, cardiometabolic dysfunction, depression, and anxiety are typically conceptualized as consequences and are generally examined as separate downstream outcomes of stress exposure throughout the lifespan, and especially in aging.

An alternative possibility we will elaborate on in this review is that, from middle adulthood onward, these conditions increasingly become part of the regulatory process that generates and maintains dysregulation.
Thus, they may not simply share stress-related causes; they may also act on one another and feed back into the same stress-related systems that contributed to their emergence.

In this review, we will discuss the idea that what appears epidemiologically as comorbidity among these stress-related health problems in late adulthood may, at least in part, reflect a self-maintaining failure of shared regulatory systems.
We move beyond comorbidity to consider cognitive decline, cardiometabolic dysfunction, depression, and anxiety in older adults as components of a potentially mutually reinforcing system.

In the next sections, (i) we examine the evidence for the directional pathways linking cognitive decline, cardiometabolic dysfunction, depressive and anxiety symptomatology (including both clinically diagnosed disorders and dimensionally at levels below diagnostic thresholds); (ii) we discuss and hypothesize how mechanisms central to stress regulation, including neurocognitive, neurovisceral and psychophysiological processes, could provide the substrate through which changes in one domain influence the others; (iii) we discuss and hypothesize how these altered processes may, at the same time, affect stressregulatory systems in aging, contributing to the maintenance of HPA axis and ANS dysregulation, and (iv) we then argue that, from middle adulthood onward, the effects of stress and allostatic load on health may be understood not only as the cumulative consequence of stress acting on the organism, but also as the accumulating expression of a regulatory system in which cognitive decline, cardiometabolic dysfunction, depression, and anxiety increasingly sustain one another as people age.

Building on findings from relatively independent fields, we aim to synthesize empirical evidence, elaborate on new mechanistic links, provide a unified perspective on how cognitive, cardiometabolic, and psychological health problems evolve as people age, and generate new research questions to guide future research.

Although the HPA axis and the ANS do not exhaust the biology of stress and aging, we focus on these two systems because they constitute rapid bidirectional regulatory interfaces through which the brain, metabolic organs, and environmental demands interact.
Immune, inflammatory, and cellular-aging processes represent closely interacting parallel pathways outside the primary scope of this framework.
>Depression and anxiety as drivers of cardiometabolic dysfunction and cognitive decline.
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Depression and anxiety as drivers of cardiometabolic dysfunction and cognitive decline.</head>

text.text: Among the directional pathways considered in this review, the contribution of stress-related psychological dysfunction to subsequent cardiometabolic and cognitive problems is arguably one of the most extensively investigated.

A large body of meta-analytic research indicates that depression predicts the later development of metabolic syndrome (MetS; a cluster of conditions including impaired glucose levels, hypertriglyceridemia, abdominal obesity, low high-density lipoprotein cholesterol levels, and hypertension; Wang et al., 2020) and its independent and related components (e.g., type 2 diabetes, insulin resistance, obesity, and other cardiovascular outcomes) (Mezuk et al., 2008; Gan et al., 2014; Cao et al., 2022).

text.text: Anxiety has received comparatively less attention but shows a similar pattern.

A meta-analysis of 37 prospective studies including more than 1.5 million individuals found that anxiety was associated with a 52% higher incidence of cardiovascular disease, independently of several conventional cardiovascular risk factors and depression (Batelaan et al., 2016).

text.text: Importantly, although the studies included in these meta-analyses spanned a wide age range (18 to 99 years), the mean age in most studies was around the fifth decade or older, and results were similar when researchers considered participants older than 65 years (Cao et al., 2022).

text.text: Still, more research is needed to understand whether LLD and LLA carry a prospective cardiometabolic risk different from that associated with depression and anxiety diagnosed in younger adulthood.

A central mechanism proposed to account for the prospective associations is that depression and anxiety (even at subclinical levels) can prolong and repeatedly activate the physiological stress response, increasing cumulative exposure to HPA-axis and autonomic dysregulation.

Depression and anxiety are characterized not only by maladaptive responses to stressors but also by psychological processes such as rumination, worry, anticipatory threat processing, and maladaptive appraisal that may maintain the representation of a stressor in the absence of the stressor itself (e.g., De Raedt and Koster, 2010; De Raedt and Hooley, 2016; Brown et al., 2023; Pulopulos et al., 2023).

text.text: The perseverative cognition hypothesis proposes that processes associated with rumination and worry prolong stress-related physiological activation over time (Brosschot et al., 2006).

text.text: Thus, depression and anxiety (clinically diagnosed but also subclinical symptomatology) may increase cardiometabolic burden by prolonging the duration and increasing the frequency of glucocorticoid, sympathetic-adrenergic, and parasympathetic responses, repeatedly engaging the metabolic and cardiovascular systems to deal with (real or imagined) stressors and leading to their impairment.
Depression and anxiety have been consistently associated with cognitive decline in aging.

In a metaanalysis, Hudon et al. (2020) observed that depressive symptoms and diagnosis of depression were incident predictors of both cognitive decline and dementia in cognitively normal middle-aged and older adults, and Santabárbara et al. (2020) showed that depression was associated with a 63% higher risk of subsequent dementia.

text.text: These associations are clearer for late-life phenotypes than for midlife.

In LLD, 20% to 50% of individuals experience cognitive impairment exceeding that of matched controls based on age and education, with processing speed and executive functions being most consistently and severely impacted (Butters et al., 2004; Sheline et al., 2006; Koenig et al., 2014; Szymkowicz et al., 2023).

text.text: Such deficits are attributed to disruption of the cognitive control network, including the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, dorsal and rostral anterior cingulate, and parietal association regions (Aizenstein et al., 2009; Alexopoulos et al., 2012; Morimoto et al., 2015).

text.text: Regarding anxiety, the evidence is less extensive but suggests a similar trend.

Meta-analytic evidence in older adults indicates that anxiety is associated with an increased risk of cognitive impairment and dementia, with stronger associations observed at higher ages (Gulpers et al., 2016).

text.text: Another possibility is that a causal relationship exists in which depression and anxiety contribute to cognitive decline in older adults.
The same processes linking depression and anxiety to cardiometabolic disorders may provide a plausible pathway from psychological dysfunction to cognitive decline.

Repeated and maladaptive activation of the HPA axis as observed in depression and anxiety may affect brain regions critical for cognition, including the prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, and amygdala, all of which contain glucocorticoid receptors and undergo functional and structural remodeling after prolonged stress (McEwen, 2002; McEwen, 2008; Lupien et al., 2018).

text.text: In humans, chronic stress, prolonged glucocorticoid exposure, and dysregulated HPA axis activity have been associated with alterations in hippocampal and prefrontal structure and function, impairing memory and executive functions (e.g., Pulopulos et al., 2014; Hidalgo et al., 2016; Pulopulos et al., 2016; Lupien et al., 2018; Montoliu et al., 2018).

text.text: Importantly, these changes may also impair the ability of the same brain regions to regulate subsequent stress responses (Baeken and De Raedt, 2011), leading to maladaptive stress regulation and exacerbating HPA axis dysregulation.

text.text: This cascade of events may provide a potential mechanism through which depression and anxiety (even subclinically) progressively compromise both cognition and stress regulation.

This mechanism is particularly relevant from middle adulthood onward, when stress-related alterations occur against a background of declining neural resilience (Reuter-Lorenz and Park, 2014) and an allostatic burden that accumulates across adulthood and remains high in later life (Crimmins et al., 2003; Juster et al., 2010).

text.text: However, although the route from prolonged or dysregulated HPA activity to cognitive decline is relatively well documented in the general population, it has not been examined prospectively in LLD and LLA, and more research is needed to understand the long-term impact of these psychological conditions on HPA regulation and its later impact on cognitive aging.
The noradrenergic system, a main component of the sympathetic system, provides a second, complementary pathway.

The locus coeruleus-noradrenaline (LC-NA) system plays an important modulatory role on the PFC and hippocampus and is essential for attention, working memory, and adaptive responding to environmental demands (Mather and Harley, 2016).

text.text: Moderate levels of NA support PFC function, whereas high tonic LC activity and high NA levels associated with intense stress recruit lower-affinity adrenergic receptors and rapidly impair PFC-dependent cognition (Arnsten, 2009; Datta and Arnsten, 2019).

text.formatted: Importantly, depression and anxiety have themselves been associated with abnormalities in the adrenergic system (for reviews, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b154">Morris et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b190">Reyes, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">Korukonda and Weinshenker, 2026)</ref>, and particularly in aging, LLD has been linked to worse structural integrity of the LC <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Guinea-Izquierdo et al., 2021)</ref> and lower functional connectivity between the LC and the anterior cingulate cortex, which correlates with the severity of depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(del Cerro et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Aging has also been linked to increased mean diffusivity in the LC in older adults (Valdés Cabrera et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Aging has also been linked to increased mean diffusivity in the LC in older adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b229">(Valdés Cabrera et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, LC microstructural integrity is linked to processing speed and executive function in aging regardless of depression status (Valdés Cabrera et al., 2026), and the functional topography of the LC changes throughout adulthood in ways associated with emotional memory and emotion regulation (Veréb et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Importantly, LC microstructural integrity is linked to processing speed and executive function in aging regardless of depression status <ref type="bibr" target="#b229">(Valdés Cabrera et al., 2026)</ref>, and the functional topography of the LC changes throughout adulthood in ways associated with emotional memory and emotion regulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b237">(Veréb et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This indicates that aging, affective dysfunction, and cognitive control all involve the same noradrenergic system.

Taken together, the epidemiological and mechanistic evidence supports depression and anxiety as important potential amplifiers of both cardiometabolic dysfunction and cognitive decline in aging, acting in part by further dysregulating the same HPA, autonomic, and central noradrenergic systems through which stress links to psychological, cognitive, and cardiometabolic conditions.
>Cardiometabolic dysfunction as a driver of depression, anxiety and cognitive decline.
text.formatted: <head n="3." >Cardiometabolic dysfunction as a driver of depression, anxiety and cognitive decline.</head>

text.text: Compared with the well-established literature linking depression and anxiety to cardiometabolic dysfunction, the opposite pathway has received less systematic attention.
Prospective epidemiological evidence indicates that the direction of influence is not exclusively psychological-to-metabolic.

Chourpiliadis et al. (2024) followed more than 200,000 individuals (mean age at baseline 42.1, SD 12.6) for a mean of 21 years and observed that higher glucose and triglyceride levels predicted a greater subsequent risk of depression, anxiety, and other stress-related disorders, whereas higher high-density lipoprotein cholesterol was associated with lower risk.
Furthermore, metabolic differences between individuals who later developed psychiatric disorders and controls were detectable up to two decades before diagnosis.
These findings suggest that metabolic abnormalities may precede the clinical emergence of depression and anxiety rather than merely arise as a consequence of it.
Importantly, Liu et al. (2022) also demonstrated that this metabolic signature is itself age-dependent.
text.formatted: Importantly, <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">Liu et al. (2022)</ref> also demonstrated that this metabolic signature is itself age-dependent.

text.text: In a community cohort of adults aged over 50, they identified seventeen plasma metabolites that were simultaneously associated with depressive symptoms and correlated with age, suggesting that the metabolic contribution to depression becomes progressively more relevant as metabolic disturbance accumulates.
This idea is also supported by evidence obtained specifically in later life.

Among 40,080 initially depression-free participants of the Swedish Twin Registry (mean age 60) followed for eighteen years, one cardiometabolic disease was associated with a 52% higher hazard of incident depression and two or more with an 83% higher hazard (Yang et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Among 40,080 initially depression-free participants of the Swedish Twin Registry (mean age 60) followed for eighteen years, one cardiometabolic disease was associated with a 52% higher hazard of incident depression and two or more with an 83% higher hazard <ref type="bibr" target="#b248">(Yang et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, the risk effect was larger when the cardiometabolic disease had developed in midlife (before age 60) than in late life, suggesting a midlife transition point.

Regarding anxiety, while evidence in LLA is limited, findings suggest that certain multimorbidity patterns involving cardiometabolic disease can predict the onset of an anxiety disorder (Palmese et al., 2026), and that cardiometabolic disorders may increase the likelihood of the first onset of internalizing disorders (including any mood or anxiety disorder) six years later in more than 4,000 participants aged 18-64 at baseline (mean age 44.3; SD=12.5) (Nuyen et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Regarding anxiety, while evidence in LLA is limited, findings suggest that certain multimorbidity patterns involving cardiometabolic disease can predict the onset of an anxiety disorder <ref type="bibr" target="#b164">(Palmese et al., 2026)</ref>, and that cardiometabolic disorders may increase the likelihood of the first onset of internalizing disorders (including any mood or anxiety disorder) six years later in more than 4,000 participants aged 18-64 at baseline (mean age 44.3; SD=12.5) <ref type="bibr" target="#b156">(Nuyen et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: However, the evidence regarding the predictive value of cardiometabolic conditions for depression and anxiety has not always been observed (e.g., Nuyen et al., 2021), which highlights the large heterogeneity in physiological profiles and health trajectories.
text.formatted: However, the evidence regarding the predictive value of cardiometabolic conditions for depression and anxiety has not always been observed (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b156">Nuyen et al., 2021)</ref>, which highlights the large heterogeneity in physiological profiles and health trajectories.

text.text: Importantly, cardiometabolic dysfunction is an umbrella domain rather than a unitary biological entity.
Different components are expected to engage different pathways and to produce partially distinct psychological and cognitive phenotypes.
Along this line, researchers have proposed different mechanisms underlying the prospective association between cardiometabolic dysfunction and depression and anxiety in aging.

The 'vascular depression' hypothesis postulates that cerebrovascular disease may predispose, precipitate, or perpetuate some geriatric depressive syndromes (characterized by retardation, anhedonia, lack of insight into their illness, and disability, and fewer reports of feelings of guilt) by impairing frontolimbic networks supporting affective processes (Alexopoulos, 2019).
Given the clinical overlap between depression, apathy, and executive-behavioral syndromes in aging, distinguishing affective distress from motivational and behavioral changes is essential.
These phenotypes may reflect partly different mechanisms and may not engage the hypothesized stress-regulatory feedback loops in equivalent ways.

Some authors have also proposed the definition of (immuno-)metabolic depression as a bio-clinical dimension defined jointly by atypical energy-related depressive symptoms (increased appetite and weight, sleep problems, fatigue, motivational impairment, and anhedonia), together with low-grade systemic inflammation and metabolic abnormality, and associated with higher cardiometabolic disease risk and with poorer response to standard antidepressant treatment (Penninx et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Some authors have also proposed the definition of (immuno-)metabolic depression as a bio-clinical dimension defined jointly by atypical energy-related depressive symptoms (increased appetite and weight, sleep problems, fatigue, motivational impairment, and anhedonia), together with low-grade systemic inflammation and metabolic abnormality, and associated with higher cardiometabolic disease risk and with poorer response to standard antidepressant treatment <ref type="bibr" target="#b167">(Penninx et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, cumulative decline across physiological systems, including endocrine-metabolic regulation, is not only a core feature of biological aging (Clegg et al., 2013), but also a major mechanism for conceptualizing LLD as a disorder of accelerated biological aging (Alexopoulos, 2019).
text.formatted: Thus, cumulative decline across physiological systems, including endocrine-metabolic regulation, is not only a core feature of biological aging <ref type="bibr">(Clegg et al., 2013)</ref>, but also a major mechanism for conceptualizing LLD as a disorder of accelerated biological aging <ref type="bibr">(Alexopoulos, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Insulin may play an important role in explaining how metabolic dysfunction may lead to depression and anxiety.
Type 2 diabetes, obesity, and MetS (and its components) are independently associated with insulin resistance, which on its own has been associated with more severe mood disorders (Meng et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Type 2 diabetes, obesity, and MetS (and its components) are independently associated with insulin resistance, which on its own has been associated with more severe mood disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b142">(Meng et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: A potential pathway involves metabolic and endocrine signaling to the brain, as insulin modulates neuronal and glial metabolism, synaptic plasticity, memory, reward, and emotional functioning.

Peripheral insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes can coexist with impaired insulin signaling in the brain, which may compromise synaptic, metabolic, and immune functions and has been implicated in both cognitive impairment and psychiatric symptoms (Arnold et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Peripheral insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes can coexist with impaired insulin signaling in the brain, which may compromise synaptic, metabolic, and immune functions and has been implicated in both cognitive impairment and psychiatric symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Arnold et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, glucose metabolism in medial prefrontal regions during psychosocial stress is associated with the magnitude of the cortisol response (Kern et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Moreover, glucose metabolism in medial prefrontal regions during psychosocial stress is associated with the magnitude of the cortisol response <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">(Kern et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Brain insulin resistance has therefore been proposed as one possible biological hub connecting metabolic dysfunction with depression and anxiety, particularly with cognitive symptoms and anhedonia (Kleinridders et al., 2015; Hamer et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Brain insulin resistance has therefore been proposed as one possible biological hub connecting metabolic dysfunction with depression and anxiety, particularly with cognitive symptoms and anhedonia <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">(Kleinridders et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Hamer et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: MetS may also promote neuroinflammation and disrupt hypothalamic regulation of hormonal balance (Van Dyken and Lacoste, 2018).
A second, less-explored pathway involves autonomic dysregulation.

MetS, obesity, insulin resistance, and hypertension are associated with increased sympathetic activity, and sympathetic overdrive has itself been proposed as an important component in the development and progression of MetS (Grassi, 2006; Schlaich et al., 2015).
text.formatted: MetS, obesity, insulin resistance, and hypertension are associated with increased sympathetic activity, and sympathetic overdrive has itself been proposed as an important component in the development and progression of MetS <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Grassi, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b201">Schlaich et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Cardiometabolic dysfunction is also associated with reduced cardiac vagal regulation (for a meta-analysis, see Ortiz-Guzmán et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Cardiometabolic dysfunction is also associated with reduced cardiac vagal regulation (for a meta-analysis, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b158">Ortiz-Guzmán et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, lower cardiac vagal control has been associated with less flexible emotional responding and less effective regulation of negative affect (Williams et al., 2015), and our research also shows that lower HRV in anticipation of a stressor is associated with a higher stress-induced cortisol response (Pulopulos et al., 2018; Pulopulos et al., 2020b).
text.formatted: Importantly, lower cardiac vagal control has been associated with less flexible emotional responding and less effective regulation of negative affect <ref type="bibr" target="#b245">(Williams et al., 2015)</ref>, and our research also shows that lower HRV in anticipation of a stressor is associated with a higher stress-induced cortisol response <ref type="bibr">(Pulopulos et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pulopulos et al., 2020b)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, we argue that the autonomic relationship may itself become bidirectional.

That is, depression and anxiety promote prolonged sympathetic activation and vagal withdrawal, as discussed in the previous section, while an increased metabolic burden may shift autonomic regulation toward sympathetic dominance and reduced vagal control, shifting the brain's stress response away from prefrontal regions toward salience regions, and potentially decreasing the physiological flexibility required for adaptive emotion and stress regulation.
A related mechanism may arise from the afferent side of autonomic and metabolic regulation.
The vagus nerve serves as a two-way communication pathway between the body and the brain.

Vagal afferents, which represent almost 80% of the vagal fibers, sense cardiometabolic signals via their endings in the viscera and relay this information to the nucleus tractus solitarius in the brainstem, which processes it and transmits it to other brain regions.

To trigger vital homeostatic reflexes essential for cardiometabolic control, these neurons send strong projections to vagal motor neurons in the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus or the nucleus ambiguus.

Additionally, they project to regions that generate sympathetic output, such as the ventrolateral medulla and the intermediolateral cell column, as well as to respiratory centers in the brainstem and pons.

They also connect indirectly to other brain regions such as the hypothalamus, amygdala, and prefrontal cortex (particularly via the LC), where peripheral information is integrated with other circuits to regulate autonomic functions and behaviors during stress responses (Holt, 2022; Boychuk and Wang, 2026; Roy and Vanderhasselt, 2026).
text.formatted: They also connect indirectly to other brain regions such as the hypothalamus, amygdala, and prefrontal cortex (particularly via the LC), where peripheral information is integrated with other circuits to regulate autonomic functions and behaviors during stress responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">(Holt, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Boychuk and Wang, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b194">Roy and Vanderhasselt, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, cardiometabolic dysfunction remodels stress systems.

Beyond the sympathetic overdrive and reduced cardiac vagal control, cardiometabolic stressors and disease states alter inhibitory GABAergic signalling within the vagal reflex circuits themselves (vagal afferents, the nucleus tractus solitarius, and vagal motor neurons), which has been proposed as a mechanism of the vagal dysfunction associated with cardiometabolic disease (Boychuk and Wang, 2026).
text.formatted: Beyond the sympathetic overdrive and reduced cardiac vagal control, cardiometabolic stressors and disease states alter inhibitory GABAergic signalling within the vagal reflex circuits themselves (vagal afferents, the nucleus tractus solitarius, and vagal motor neurons), which has been proposed as a mechanism of the vagal dysfunction associated with cardiometabolic disease <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Boychuk and Wang, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, vagal afferent pathways transmit nutrient-, glucose-, gastrointestinal-, and hormone-related signals that are critical for regulating energy and glucose homeostasis (Waise et al., 2018; Borgmann and Fenselau, 2024).
text.formatted: Moreover, vagal afferent pathways transmit nutrient-, glucose-, gastrointestinal-, and hormone-related signals that are critical for regulating energy and glucose homeostasis <ref type="bibr" target="#b240">(Waise et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Borgmann and Fenselau, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: These neurometabolic interfaces become dysfunctional in conditions such as obesity and diabetes (Masi et al., 2018).
text.formatted: These neurometabolic interfaces become dysfunctional in conditions such as obesity and diabetes <ref type="bibr" target="#b129">(Masi et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: We therefore hypothesize that in individuals with accumulating cardiometabolic burden, the same objective stressor elicits a less flexible and less well-timed HPA-axis and autonomic response, with less capacity to recruit the prefrontal resources needed to regulate it.
Recent theoretical works provide a framework for understanding how such alterations could lead, in the long term, to depression and anxiety.

The interoceptive energy-allostasis model proposes that the brain continuously integrates peripheral metabolic signals with contextual information and previous experience to estimate the body's energetic state and prospectively regulate physiological resources (Mehrhof et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The interoceptive energy-allostasis model proposes that the brain continuously integrates peripheral metabolic signals with contextual information and previous experience to estimate the body's energetic state and prospectively regulate physiological resources <ref type="bibr" target="#b140">(Mehrhof et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Within this framework, metabolic dysfunction could alter either the peripheral signals available to the brain or their central interpretation, thereby degrading the internal model that underpins allostatic regulation.
Inaccurate or unreliable information about energetic states could consequently affect motivation, reward, effort allocation, affective experience, and subsequent physiological regulation.

Crucially, the consequence would be that cardiometabolic dysfunction could impair the feedback information the brain uses to regulate both metabolism and psychological responses in emotional and stressful situations, creating conditions in which metabolic and psychological dysfunction reinforce one another.
This self-reinforcing process would sustain less flexible autonomic and HPA axis regulation, maintaining or exacerbating their dysregulation.

This perspective also aligns with predictive allostatic-interoceptive frameworks, which propose that disruptions in integrating central predictions and peripheral bodily signals may compromise adaptive physiological regulation across psychiatric and neurological disorders (Santamaría-García et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This perspective also aligns with predictive allostatic-interoceptive frameworks, which propose that disruptions in integrating central predictions and peripheral bodily signals may compromise adaptive physiological regulation across psychiatric and neurological disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b198">(Santamaría-García et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, evidence from behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia suggests that alterations in interoceptive brain responses are associated with cognitive and affective impairments, as well as structural and functional abnormalities in the allostatic-interoceptive network. (Birba et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Similarly, evidence from behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia suggests that alterations in interoceptive brain responses are associated with cognitive and affective impairments, as well as structural and functional abnormalities in the allostatic-interoceptive network. <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Birba et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: MetS and related components (e.g., type 2 diabetes, insulin resistance, hypertension, obesity, and other vascular risk factors) have repeatedly been associated with poorer cognitive functioning and an increased risk of cognitive impairment and dementia (Henn et al., 2022).
text.formatted: MetS and related components (e.g., type 2 diabetes, insulin resistance, hypertension, obesity, and other vascular risk factors) have repeatedly been associated with poorer cognitive functioning and an increased risk of cognitive impairment and dementia <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Henn et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, Qureshi et al. (2024) showed in 37,395 dementia-free adults from the UK Biobank database that MetS was associated with lower total brain, gray matter, and hippocampal volumes, and that participants with MetS performed worse on cognitive tests of executive function, verbal declarative memory, processing speed, and verbal and nonverbal reasoning.
text.formatted: For instance, <ref type="bibr" target="#b184">Qureshi et al. (2024)</ref> showed in 37,395 dementia-free adults from the UK Biobank database that MetS was associated with lower total brain, gray matter, and hippocampal volumes, and that participants with MetS performed worse on cognitive tests of executive function, verbal declarative memory, processing speed, and verbal and nonverbal reasoning.

text.text: More MetS components were also associated with lower brain volume, greater white matter hyperintensity, and poorer cognition across all domains.
Similarly, about one in three patients with cardiac disease shows cognitive impairment, most often affecting executive functions and memory (van Nieuwkerk et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Similarly, about one in three patients with cardiac disease shows cognitive impairment, most often affecting executive functions and memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b236">(van Nieuwkerk et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Longitudinal studies suggest that these associations already become evident in middle-aged adults.

In the Framingham Offspring Study, both midlife and late-life MetS were associated with poorer cognitive functioning, with midlife MetS already associated with poorer cognition around age 55 (Bangen et al., 2019).
text.formatted: In the Framingham Offspring Study, both midlife and late-life MetS were associated with poorer cognitive functioning, with midlife MetS already associated with poorer cognition around age 55 <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bangen et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: More recently, the Guangzhou Biobank Cohort Study followed 7,775 middle-aged and older adults for up to 12 years and found that a higher MetS index was associated with faster decline in delayed recall and global cognition (MMSE), including attention and calculation, whereas persistently elevated MetS trajectories were associated with faster memory decline (Tian et al., 2025).
text.formatted: More recently, the Guangzhou Biobank Cohort Study followed 7,775 middle-aged and older adults for up to 12 years and found that a higher MetS index was associated with faster decline in delayed recall and global cognition (MMSE), including attention and calculation, whereas persistently elevated MetS trajectories were associated with faster memory decline <ref type="bibr" target="#b224">(Tian et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In a meta-analysis, González-Castañeda et al. ( 2021)also observed lower global cognitive scores in adults with MetS than those without MetS.
text.formatted: In a meta-analysis, González-Castañeda et al. ( <ref type="formula">2021)</ref>also observed lower global cognitive scores in adults with MetS than those without MetS.

text.text: Moreover, pooled data from four cohorts in China, the United Kingdom, the United States, and continental Europe (n = 40,883, mean age 63.4) showed that cardiometabolic multimorbidity is associated with worse levels and faster deterioration of physical disability, depressive symptoms, and cognitive function, with the highest odds observed for concurrent worsening across all three functional domains rather than for deterioration in any single domain (Zhang et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Moreover, pooled data from four cohorts in China, the United Kingdom, the United States, and continental Europe (n = 40,883, mean age 63.4) showed that cardiometabolic multimorbidity is associated with worse levels and faster deterioration of physical disability, depressive symptoms, and cognitive function, with the highest odds observed for concurrent worsening across all three functional domains rather than for deterioration in any single domain <ref type="bibr" target="#b254">(Zhang et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These results are in line with the idea that the psychological and cognitive consequences of cardiometabolic dysfunction occur in parallel, rather than in a fixed sequence.

Nevertheless, some studies report weaker associations than initially hypothesized, and results show high interindividual variability (e.g., Siervo et al., 2014; Koutsonida et al., 2022), suggesting that other factors may contribute to the link between cardiometabolic conditions and cognitive decline.
text.formatted: Nevertheless, some studies report weaker associations than initially hypothesized, and results show high interindividual variability (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b206">Siervo et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">Koutsonida et al., 2022)</ref>, suggesting that other factors may contribute to the link between cardiometabolic conditions and cognitive decline.

text.text: Together, the current evidence suggests that early disruptions in systemic metabolism can cause persistent and progressive effects on cognition later in life.
However, the precise mechanisms leading to cognitive impairment are still not fully understood.
Several interrelated mechanisms may account for these associations.

Cardiometabolic dysfunction contributes to cerebral small-vessel disease, endothelial dysfunction, impaired cerebrovascular reactivity and cerebral perfusion, blood-brain barrier disruption, glial disruption and inflammation, while insulin resistance may also disrupt insulin signaling and glucose metabolism within the brain (Alfaro et al., 2018; Arnold et al., 2018; Horton and Barrett, 2021; Al Haj Ahmad et al., 2022; Henn et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023; Jost and Kujach, 2025).
text.formatted: Cardiometabolic dysfunction contributes to cerebral small-vessel disease, endothelial dysfunction, impaired cerebrovascular reactivity and cerebral perfusion, blood-brain barrier disruption, glial disruption and inflammation, while insulin resistance may also disrupt insulin signaling and glucose metabolism within the brain <ref type="bibr">(Alfaro et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Arnold et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Horton and Barrett, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Al Haj Ahmad et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Henn et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b118">Li et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Jost and Kujach, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These cardiometabolic dysfunctions may compromise the brain's ability to obtain and dynamically allocate the metabolic resources required to cope with cognitive challenges.

Insulin resistance has also been associated with lower cerebral glucose metabolism, including in prefrontal, parietal, and medial temporal regions, and with poorer working, immediate, and verbal memory (Willette et al., 2015; Deery et al., 2024a).
text.formatted: Insulin resistance has also been associated with lower cerebral glucose metabolism, including in prefrontal, parietal, and medial temporal regions, and with poorer working, immediate, and verbal memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b244">(Willette et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Deery et al., 2024a)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, insulin resistance and aging also alter the coupling between cerebral blood flow and glucose metabolism, suggesting reduced efficiency in the mechanisms that supply energetic resources to the brain (Deery et al., 2024b).
text.formatted: Importantly, insulin resistance and aging also alter the coupling between cerebral blood flow and glucose metabolism, suggesting reduced efficiency in the mechanisms that supply energetic resources to the brain <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Deery et al., 2024b)</ref>.

text.text: We propose that cardiometabolic dysfunction may also affect stress-related biological systems that are crucial to cognitive performance.

The same supply mechanisms meet the energetic demands of cognitive work and the stress response because both cognitive performance and adaptive stress responses require the brain to dynamically allocate resources between central cognitive processes and peripheral physiological systems (Pulopulos et al., 2020a; Van Boven et al., 2026).
text.formatted: The same supply mechanisms meet the energetic demands of cognitive work and the stress response because both cognitive performance and adaptive stress responses require the brain to dynamically allocate resources between central cognitive processes and peripheral physiological systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b182">(Pulopulos et al., 2020a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b230">Van Boven et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Prefrontal regions particularly regulate this brainbody interaction, coordinating these adjustments through interactions with the central autonomic network (including the LC-NA system) and vagal pathways (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; McKlveen et al., 2015; Smith et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Prefrontal regions particularly regulate this brainbody interaction, coordinating these adjustments through interactions with the central autonomic network (including the LC-NA system) and vagal pathways <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b139">McKlveen et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b212">Smith et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: As described above, these systems are crucial for cognitive processes, particularly prefrontal-related executive processes.

Evidence for this coupling comes from a study with 389 patients with stable coronary artery disease showing that greater stress-induced peripheral vasoconstriction, higher inferior frontal lobe activation, and larger increases in norepinephrine and interleukin-6 were each independently associated with worse switching performance (as measured by the Trail Making Test B), and each also predicted the decline in executive function over the following two years (Moazzami et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Evidence for this coupling comes from a study with 389 patients with stable coronary artery disease showing that greater stress-induced peripheral vasoconstriction, higher inferior frontal lobe activation, and larger increases in norepinephrine and interleukin-6 were each independently associated with worse switching performance (as measured by the Trail Making Test B), and each also predicted the decline in executive function over the following two years <ref type="bibr" target="#b150">(Moazzami et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Neuroimaging evidence shows that in patients with coronary artery disease, stress-induced peripheral vasoconstriction is accompanied by increased perfusion of the insula and parietal cortex, along with decreased perfusion of the medial prefrontal cortex (Shah et al., 2019; see Wang et al., 2025 for a review).
text.formatted: Neuroimaging evidence shows that in patients with coronary artery disease, stress-induced peripheral vasoconstriction is accompanied by increased perfusion of the insula and parietal cortex, along with decreased perfusion of the medial prefrontal cortex <ref type="bibr" target="#b204">(Shah et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">see Wang et al., 2025</ref> for a review).

text.text: As mentioned above, cardiometabolic disease may therefore shift the brain's stress response away from prefrontal regions that coordinate regulation and toward salience regions.

Together, these findings support the idea that cardiometabolic dysfunction, by compromising prefrontal control and autonomic flexibility, may reduce the capacity of prefrontal systems to recruit the resources necessary for adaptive cognitive and physiological regulation during stress.
>Cognitive decline as a driver of depression, anxiety and cardiometabolic dysfunction.
text.formatted: <head n="4." >Cognitive decline as a driver of depression, anxiety and cardiometabolic dysfunction.</head>

text.text: Among the pathways considered in this review, the possibility that cognitive decline in aging contributes to subsequent depression and anxiety in aging has received comparatively less attention.

This is particularly striking for executive functions (working memory, switching, and inhibition), which are among the most affected by aging and stress, and are considered fundamental regulatory capacities required to adapt thoughts, emotions, and behavior to changing demands (De Raedt and Koster, 2010; De Raedt and Hooley, 2016; Pulopulos et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This is particularly striking for executive functions (working memory, switching, and inhibition), which are among the most affected by aging and stress, and are considered fundamental regulatory capacities required to adapt thoughts, emotions, and behavior to changing demands <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(De Raedt and Koster, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">De Raedt and Hooley, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b181">Pulopulos et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, because of their cross-cutting role in standardized cognitive tasks, declines in executive function can affect performance in other cognitive domains and contribute to global cognitive decline (Crawford et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Moreover, because of their cross-cutting role in standardized cognitive tasks, declines in executive function can affect performance in other cognitive domains and contribute to global cognitive decline <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Crawford et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">Lee et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, the question here is not whether individuals with lower cognitive ability have poorer health (a relationship examined extensively; see e.g., Batty et al., 2007; Deary, 2010) but whether within-person decline in executive functions from middle adulthood onward, particularly when it exceeds what would be expected for age, leads to psychological and cardiometabolic health problems.
text.formatted: Importantly, the question here is not whether individuals with lower cognitive ability have poorer health (a relationship examined extensively; see e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Batty et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Deary, 2010)</ref> but whether within-person decline in executive functions from middle adulthood onward, particularly when it exceeds what would be expected for age, leads to psychological and cardiometabolic health problems.

text.text: Evidence in middle-aged and older populations is consistent with this hypothesis, although it remains mixed and has rarely focused specifically on executive function.

In the Leiden 85-plus Study, poorer baseline performance on the Stroop test (reflecting interference control) and on immediate and delayed memory predicted an accelerated increase in depressive symptoms over four years (Vinkers et al., 2004).
text.formatted: In the Leiden 85-plus Study, poorer baseline performance on the Stroop test (reflecting interference control) and on immediate and delayed memory predicted an accelerated increase in depressive symptoms over four years <ref type="bibr" target="#b238">(Vinkers et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Using ten years of data from more than 16,000 adults aged ≥65, poorer prior global cognition predicted subsequent increases in depressive symptoms, with sleep quality partially mediating that path (Guo et al., 2022), and a symptom-level cross-lagged network analysis to three waves collected in 2015, 2018, and 2020 of 14,961 adults aged ≥45 found that memory and orientation predicted future depressive symptoms (Ma et al., 2025).

text.text: In 2,605 participants (mean age 55, range 33-84) followed for approximately nine years, poorer inhibition, set-shifting, working-memory updating, inductive reasoning, and global cognition each predicted generalized anxiety disorder at follow-up (Zainal and Newman, 2018).

text.text: Together, these studies suggest that associations between depression or anxiety and cognitive performance are most consistently observed when executive functions are specifically assessed, whereas they tend to be weaker or absent when cognition is assessed using global cognitive screening measures or episodic memory tests.

Research focused on mechanisms underlying the association between cognitive decline and depression and anxiety is scarce in older adults, but the evidence from younger populations provides an important starting point.

Experimental and theoretical evidence proposes that executive functions support inhibiting irrelevant or negative information, switching away from maladaptive thought patterns, updating representations as circumstances change, and maintaining goal-relevant information during stressful situations (e.g., De Raedt and Koster, 2010; De Raedt and Hooley, 2016; Vanderhasselt et al., 2023; De Smet et al., 2024).

text.text: Along these lines, a depression-executive dysfunction syndrome has been described in older adults characterized by anhedonia, psychomotor retardation, pronounced disability, lack of insight, suspiciousness, and mild vegetative syndrome, associated with worse performance in tests of verbal fluency (often conceptualized as measuring executive functioning; e.g., Henry & Crawford, 2005a , 2005b; Lezak et al., 2012), response inhibition, novel problem solving, cognitive flexibility, working memory, and/or ideomotor planning, and consistent with disruption of frontal-subcortical networks (Alexopoulos, 2019).

text.text: No study has investigated how executive function predicts changes in stress perception and regulation in aging.

However, cross-sectional evidence indicates that worse working memory, inhibition, and shifting are linked to more perceived stress in middleaged and older adults (Caswell et al., 2003; Korten et al., 2017; Pertl et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2018; Guevara et al., 2019; D'Amico et al., 2021).

text.text: As discussed above, perseverative cognition provides an established mechanism through which psychological stress extends HPA-axis and autonomic activation over time.

Together, executive functions may influence psychological health by shaping how much stress individuals generate, how they appraise it, and how long its cognitive representation persists after the event ends.
Cognitive decline could therefore enter the allostatic process upstream of psychological stress dysregulation, rather than functioning exclusively as a downstream consequence.
The contribution of cognitive functioning to stress regulation may extend beyond executive control.

Socio-affective processes, such as recognizing emotional signals, interpreting others' intentions, and adapting behavior to interpersonal situations, may also shape the appraisal and generation of social stressors but have been overlooked (Hostinar et al., 2014; Saxbe et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Socio-affective processes, such as recognizing emotional signals, interpreting others' intentions, and adapting behavior to interpersonal situations, may also shape the appraisal and generation of social stressors but have been overlooked <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(Hostinar et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b200">Saxbe et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Impairments in these processes could contribute to interpersonal misunderstandings, conflicts, or reduced social support, potentially increasing exposure to stress and limiting opportunities for interpersonal emotion regulation (Vanderhasselt et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Impairments in these processes could contribute to interpersonal misunderstandings, conflicts, or reduced social support, potentially increasing exposure to stress and limiting opportunities for interpersonal emotion regulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b235">(Vanderhasselt et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, alterations in socio-affective functioning and their interpersonal consequences may represent an additional, yet insufficiently investigated, pathway through which cognitive changes contribute to stress-system dysregulation (Saxbe et al., 2020), which may, in turn, lead to depression and anxiety disorders (Vanderhasselt et al., 2025).

text.text: Beyond these behavioral and interpersonal pathways, another potential mechanism involves prefrontal regulation of the HPA axis and autonomic functioning.
Executive function and physiological stress regulation depend partly on overlapping prefrontal systems.

The medial and lateral PFC contribute to executive control and emotion regulation while also regulating autonomic and neuroendocrine responses through interactions with the amygdala, hypothalamus, brainstem, LC-NA system, and vagal pathways (McKlveen et al., 2015; Smith et al., 2017; De Wandel et al., 2020; Razza et al., 2024; Van Boven et al., 2026; Keppens et al., 2026).

text.text: Several lines of evidence support close coupling between executive function demands and these neurovisceral systems.
The LC-NA system plays a central role in executive function and adapts noradrenergic signaling as task demands change (Grueschow et al., 2020).

text.text: Anticipating cognitive and physical effort is accompanied by dorsomedial PFC activity and pupil dilation (a marker associated with the LC-NA system), consistent with anticipatory central energization (Kurniawan et al., 2021; Pulopulos et al., 2022; Van Boven et al., 2026).
