text.text: Experimentally modulating the DLPFC can alter effort-related cardiovascular mobilization during demanding cognitive performance (Framorando et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Experimentally modulating the DLPFC can alter effort-related cardiovascular mobilization during demanding cognitive performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Framorando et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, increasing executive demands produces phasic cardiac vagal withdrawal, and the magnitude of this withdrawal moderates the relationship between cognitive performance and PFC hemodynamic recruitment (Wei et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Similarly, increasing executive demands produces phasic cardiac vagal withdrawal, and the magnitude of this withdrawal moderates the relationship between cognitive performance and PFC hemodynamic recruitment <ref type="bibr" target="#b243">(Wei et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these findings indicate that successful executive function involves dynamic coordination between prefrontal activity, central noradrenergic signaling, and peripheral autonomic regulation rather than cognition operating independently of physiological resource allocation.

We propose that age-related deterioration of prefrontal-related cognitive-control systems may progressively reduce the efficiency of this coordination, a process that may be exacerbated by stress exposure throughout the lifespan.
As prefrontal regulatory capacity declines, the organism may become less able to match central and peripheral resource mobilization to actual environmental demands.
Reduced topdown control could result in less flexible LC-NA activity, inappropriate vagal withdrawal or recovery, and less precise modulation of HPA-axis responses.
The consequence might not be a constant increase in activation of all stress systems.
Instead, it would involve a loss of regulation that depends on the context, leading to activation that is excessive, too little, mistimed, or lasts longer than needed relative to the real demands.

From this perspective, prefrontal-related cognitive control decline could contribute simultaneously to psychological dysfunction (through poorer appraisal, emotion regulation, perseverative cognition, socioaffective processes) and to physiological dysregulation through increasingly inefficient neurovisceral control, which will ultimately lead to psychological disorders such as depression and anxiety.

Although cognitive functioning is usually treated as an outcome of cardiometabolic health, a separate epidemiological literature indicates that cognition can also precede metabolic and cardiovascular outcomes. Vishwanath et al. (2026) examined cognitive trajectories before incident cardiovascular events in 9,435 initially cardiovascular disease-free older adults from the Aspirin in Reducing Events in the Elderly randomized clinical trial and the extension observational study.

(2026)</ref> examined cognitive trajectories before incident cardiovascular events in 9,435 initially cardiovascular disease-free older adults from the Aspirin in Reducing Events in the Elderly randomized clinical trial and the extension observational study.

text.text: Individuals who subsequently experienced a cardiovascular event showed faster cognitive decline several years before the event.

Importantly for this framework, composite executive function declined significantly faster in future cardiovascular disease cases, with trajectories beginning to diverge about six years before the cardiovascular event.

These findings provide important evidence that changes in cognition, particularly executive functioning, precede clinically manifest cardiovascular disease. Leng et al. (2018) reported similar results in the Women's Health Initiative Memory Study.
text.formatted: These findings provide important evidence that changes in cognition, particularly executive functioning, precede clinically manifest cardiovascular disease. <ref type="bibr" target="#b113">Leng et al. (2018)</ref> reported similar results in the Women's Health Initiative Memory Study.

text.text: Among 5,596 women aged 60 and over who were free of cardiovascular disease at baseline and followed for an average of 7.1 years, every 5-point lower baseline score on the Modified Mini-Mental State Examination was associated with a 12% higher risk of incident cardiovascular disease, a 37% higher risk of heart failure, a 35% higher risk of cardiovascular death and a 24% higher risk of all-cause mortality.

More importantly, every additional 1-point-per-year decline was associated with a 4% higher risk of incident cardiovascular disease, 10% for coronary heart disease, 9% for stroke or transient ischaemic attack, 17% for cardiovascular death and 13% for all-cause mortality.

One proposed explanation for this prospective association is that subclinical vascular pathology could already be present years before clinical diagnosis and could simultaneously impair cognition and increase cardiovascular risk (Vishwanath et al., 2026).
text.formatted: One proposed explanation for this prospective association is that subclinical vascular pathology could already be present years before clinical diagnosis and could simultaneously impair cognition and increase cardiovascular risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b239">(Vishwanath et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, this explanation is compatible with the vascular mechanisms discussed in the previous sections.
However, at least three other mechanisms could translate declining executive function into greater cardiometabolic risk.
The first is behavioral.

Managing cardiometabolic risk successfully requires planning, prospective memory, inhibition of habitual behavior, updating health information, medication adherence, symptom monitoring, and sustained regulation of diet and physical activity.

A systematic review concluded that poorer executive function and other cognitive abilities in older adults with type 2 diabetes are associated with poorer medication adherence, glucose monitoring, appointment attendance, insulin-management skills, and other self-care behaviors (Tomlin and Sinclair, 2016).
text.formatted: A systematic review concluded that poorer executive function and other cognitive abilities in older adults with type 2 diabetes are associated with poorer medication adherence, glucose monitoring, appointment attendance, insulin-management skills, and other self-care behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b225">(Tomlin and Sinclair, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Likewise, in heart failure, cognitive impairment is associated with poorer treatment adherence and self-care, and cardiac patients with cognitive impairment experience more recurrent cardiovascular events, which are in turn associated with further cognitive decline (van Nieuwkerk et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Likewise, in heart failure, cognitive impairment is associated with poorer treatment adherence and self-care, and cardiac patients with cognitive impairment experience more recurrent cardiovascular events, which are in turn associated with further cognitive decline <ref type="bibr" target="#b236">(van Nieuwkerk et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, meta-analytic evidence indicates that the effect of executive function on health behavior is modest (Gray-Burrows et al., 2019), and other factors may also play an important role.
text.formatted: However, meta-analytic evidence indicates that the effect of executive function on health behavior is modest <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Gray-Burrows et al., 2019)</ref>, and other factors may also play an important role.

text.text: In this context, while cognitive abilities may influence health-related behaviors, their translation into effective disease management likely depends on contextual (i.e., sociological) resources, including access to healthcare, social support, and opportunities to implement recommended behaviors.
The second mechanism is the stress-regulatory pathway described in the previous sections.

We argue that reduced prefrontal control and executive function may increase perceived stress and perseverative cognition, extending HPA-axis and autonomic activation (Pulopulos et al., 2019; Pulopulos et al., 2020a; Pulopulos et al., 2023), increasing allostatic load and leading to cardiometabolic dysfunction (Ortiz et al., 2022).
text.formatted: We argue that reduced prefrontal control and executive function may increase perceived stress and perseverative cognition, extending HPA-axis and autonomic activation <ref type="bibr" target="#b178">(Pulopulos et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b182">Pulopulos et al., 2020a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b181">Pulopulos et al., 2023)</ref>, increasing allostatic load and leading to cardiometabolic dysfunction <ref type="bibr" target="#b159">(Ortiz et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The third mechanism involves the neurovisceral pathway.

We hypothesize that declining prefrontal regulatory capacity may itself contribute to increasingly inefficient autonomic, noradrenergic, and HPA-axis regulation, producing repeated unnecessary or mistimed central vs peripheral metabolic mobilization.

This pathway is supported by neuromodulation studies showing that increasing prefrontal activity (particularly dorsolateral and medial regions) increases HPA axis regulation under stress, but also noradrenergic and parasympathetic regulation during executive control tasks, and baroreflex function (a central-peripheral system involved in the control of blood pressure) (Pulopulos et al., 2020a; Razza et al., 2024; van Boven et al., 2026; Montoro et al., 2025; Keppens et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This pathway is supported by neuromodulation studies showing that increasing prefrontal activity (particularly dorsolateral and medial regions) increases HPA axis regulation under stress, but also noradrenergic and parasympathetic regulation during executive control tasks, and baroreflex function (a central-peripheral system involved in the control of blood pressure) <ref type="bibr" target="#b182">(Pulopulos et al., 2020a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b187">Razza et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">van Boven et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b152">Montoro et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">Keppens et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, deterioration of the prefrontal systems supporting cognitive control may reduce the efficiency with which metabolic resources are dynamically allocated between central and peripheral systems during challenge.
Over time, these processes could contribute to the allostatic burden that promotes insulin resistance, hypertension, endothelial dysfunction, and other cardiometabolic dysfunctions.
Taken together, the available evidence suggests that cognitive functioning should not be considered exclusively a downstream consequence of psychological and cardiometabolic problems.
Cognitive decline (particularly executive functions) may represent a turning point in the transition from accumulated allostatic burden to self-maintaining dysregulation.

As the regulatory capacity required to manage stress begins to deteriorate, psychological and cardiometabolic dysfunction may become progressively more capable of sustaining (and being sustained by) the same failing regulatory system.
Importantly, we do not propose that executive dysfunction captures the full cognitive-aging phenotype.

Rather, among cognitive functions, executive control is particularly relevant to the present framework because it directly participates in appraisal, emotion regulation, behavioral self-regulation, socio-affective processes, and neurovisceral control.
The mechanisms described above explain how depression, anxiety, cognitive decline, and cardiometabolic dysfunction may affect one another.

Importantly, we want to emphasize that these mechanisms may also negatively affect HPA axis and ANS regulation, thereby sustaining dysregulation of the biological stress systems responsible for these conditions (Figure 1).

text.text: The cardiometabolic node may act on the same systems from the periphery.

Autonomic dysregulation, as reflected in sympathetic overactivity and diminished cardiac vagal control, is not only linked to metabolic syndrome but is considered an integral part of it (Grassi, 2006; Schlaich et al., 2015; Ortiz-Guzman et al., 2023).

text.text: Vagal activity, in turn, exerts an inhibitory influence over glucose regulation, HPA-axis activity, sympathetic activation, and inflammatory processes, with the prefrontal cortex and amygdala as the central structures linking these systems to the vagus (Thayer and Sternberg, 2006; Pulopulos et al., 2018; Pulopulos et al., 2020b; Keppens et al., 2026).

text.text: Reduced vagal control can therefore increase HPA axis and sympathetic activity, contributing to their dysregulation.

Regarding cognitive decline, executive function impairment may alter stress perception and regulation (e.g., Osmanovic-Thunström et al., 2015; Pertl et al., 2017; Korten et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2018; Guevara et al., 2019; D'Amico et al., 2021), and perseverative cognition (De Lissnyder et al., 2012; Snyder and Hankin, 2016; Ng et al., 2022), increasing HPA axis and ANS activation.

text.text: Moreover, prefrontal cortex-related control is crucial for context-sensitive vagal, sympathoadrenal, and HPA-axis responses to challenges (e.g., Pulopulos et al., 2020a; Framorando et al., 2021; van Boven et al., 2026).

text.text: The effects extend beyond the individual through interpersonal regulatory processes.

Changes in cognitive and affective functioning can modify social behavior and relationship dynamics, potentially generating additional stressors or reducing opportunities for interpersonal emotion regulation.
In turn, these changes in the social environment may influence subsequent psychological and physiological responses (Vanderhasselt et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In turn, these changes in the social environment may influence subsequent psychological and physiological responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b235">(Vanderhasselt et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Together, dysregulation of the HPA axis and ANS should be seen as both a cause and a consequence of the feedback loop.

From this perspective, accelerated biological aging linked to depression, anxiety, cognitive decline, and cardiometabolic dysfunction is not only caused or exacerbated by stress but is also sustained internally by a regulatory system whose failures contribute to its own inputs (see Figure 1).

text.text: The framework proposed here raises an important question: when do psychological, cognitive, and cardiometabolic problems begin to operate as a mutually reinforcing system?

We propose that during middle adulthood (between the fourth and sixth decades of life), several processes that have previously developed relatively independently increasingly overlap, creating conditions in which reciprocal influences may become progressively stronger and coupling increases.
Middle adulthood may represent a particularly likely transition period.
Several observations make middle adulthood a plausible candidate for such a transition.

First, although changes in the HPA axis and ANS are frequently observed in older adults, these changes are progressive, with pronounced dysregulation emerging in middle adulthood, around the fifth decade of life (Jandackova et al., 2016; Thayer et al., 2021; Miller et al., 2016).
text.formatted: First, although changes in the HPA axis and ANS are frequently observed in older adults, these changes are progressive, with pronounced dysregulation emerging in middle adulthood, around the fifth decade of life <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">(Jandackova et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b223">Thayer et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b148">Miller et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Second, cardiometabolic burden increases markedly during this period.

As noted above, the prevalence of MetS in US adults is approximately twice as high at ages 40-59 as at ages 20-39 (Hirode and Wong, 2020), while many of its components (including insulin resistance, hypertension, visceral adiposity, and vascular dysfunction) may remain subclinical for years before producing overt disease.

text.text: Third, subtle reductions in cognitive functioning, including reasoning and executive processes, can be detected from the fifth decade onward, even though most individuals remain cognitively healthy and can compensate for these changes (Singh-Manoux et al., 2012; Reuter-Lorenz and Park, 2014).
text.formatted: Third, subtle reductions in cognitive functioning, including reasoning and executive processes, can be detected from the fifth decade onward, even though most individuals remain cognitively healthy and can compensate for these changes <ref type="bibr" target="#b210">(Singh-Manoux et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b189">Reuter-Lorenz and Park, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Fourth, the physiological consequences of cumulative stress exposure are becoming increasingly apparent in this period.
In a classic population-based analysis, allostatic load increased sharply between young adulthood and approximately age 60 before reaching a relative plateau at older ages (Crimmins et al., 2003).
text.formatted: In a classic population-based analysis, allostatic load increased sharply between young adulthood and approximately age 60 before reaching a relative plateau at older ages <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Crimmins et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Midlife also involves the coexistence of multiple social roles and demands, including work, parenting, and, for many individuals, caregiving for aging relatives, increasing exposure to stressors (Lachman, 2004; Lachman et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Midlife also involves the coexistence of multiple social roles and demands, including work, parenting, and, for many individuals, caregiving for aging relatives, increasing exposure to stressors <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">(Lachman, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">Lachman et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, recent evidence suggests that neural aging itself may also change during this period. Antal et al. (2025) examined the organization of functional brain networks in over 19,000 participants and found that these networks become increasingly unstable throughout life, and that this destabilization follows a nonlinear pattern, with identifiable temporal milestones of brain aging beginning in midlife (the 40s).
text.formatted: Finally, recent evidence suggests that neural aging itself may also change during this period. <ref type="bibr">Antal et al. (2025)</ref> examined the organization of functional brain networks in over 19,000 participants and found that these networks become increasingly unstable throughout life, and that this destabilization follows a nonlinear pattern, with identifiable temporal milestones of brain aging beginning in midlife (the 40s).

text.text: We therefore propose that in young adulthood, the relative preservation of cognitive control, metabolic flexibility, and physiological reserve serves as a buffer, preventing disruptions in any one area from spreading systemically.
In middle adulthood, accumulated stress often coincides with increased cardiometabolic burdens, along with slight declines in executive control and neurovisceral regulation capacity.
This can make perturbations propagate more easily, with psychological, cardiometabolic, and cognitive issues affecting each other and the HPA axis and ANS systems.
These mutual influences may become deeply integrated, resulting in synergistic effects (e.g., Khambaty et al., 2022).
text.formatted: These mutual influences may become deeply integrated, resulting in synergistic effects (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">Khambaty et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, as people age, psychological, cognitive, and metabolic dysfunction not only rises and worsens with stress, but their mutual interactions also strengthen.
Longitudinal studies beginning in middle adulthood are therefore particularly important because they can capture the formation of the loop rather than only its consequences.

Importantly, increasing coupling among these domains does not imply that psychological (depression and anxiety), cognitive, and cardiometabolic conditions will necessarily deteriorate together in every individual.
Indeed, research has shown that the profile of these age-related conditions is heterogeneous (Kokkeler et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022; Szymkowicz et al., 2023; Maksyutynska et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Indeed, research has shown that the profile of these age-related conditions is heterogeneous <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">(Kokkeler et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">Liu et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b218">Szymkowicz et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b126">Maksyutynska et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In some individuals, the predominant coupling may occur between cognitive decline and depression or anxiety, whereas in others, psychological and cardiometabolic conditions or cognitive and cardiometabolic deterioration may become more strongly interconnected.
Some individuals may show relatively isolated dysfunction within a single domain, with limited propagation to the others.
We propose that these different trajectories may reflect variation in the availability of protective and compensatory resources that can interrupt or weaken cross-domain feedback.

We recently proposed that factors such as physical activity, diet, sleep, social connectedness, socioeconomic resources, and engagement in cognitively (including socially) stimulating activities may preserve physiological and cognitive regulatory capacity (Vanderhasselt et al., 2025), thereby reducing the likelihood that dysfunction in one domain spreads to another.
text.formatted: We recently proposed that factors such as physical activity, diet, sleep, social connectedness, socioeconomic resources, and engagement in cognitively (including socially) stimulating activities may preserve physiological and cognitive regulatory capacity <ref type="bibr" target="#b235">(Vanderhasselt et al., 2025)</ref>, thereby reducing the likelihood that dysfunction in one domain spreads to another.

text.text: This idea is consistent with the revised Scaffolding Theory of Aging and Cognition, which emphasizes that trajectories of cognitive aging emerge from the balance between age-and disease-related neural challenges and compensatory or protective influences, including cognitive reserve, neural resource enrichment, physical activity, intellectual engagement, and other life-course exposures (Reuter-Lorenz and Park, 2014).
text.formatted: This idea is consistent with the revised Scaffolding Theory of Aging and Cognition, which emphasizes that trajectories of cognitive aging emerge from the balance between age-and disease-related neural challenges and compensatory or protective influences, including cognitive reserve, neural resource enrichment, physical activity, intellectual engagement, and other life-course exposures <ref type="bibr" target="#b189">(Reuter-Lorenz and Park, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, social and socioeconomic conditions may not only act as protective or compensatory resources but may also shape the chronic environmental demands to which individuals must adapt.
Recent allostaticinteroceptive frameworks have emphasized the integration of biological regulation with social and environmental adversity (Migeot and Ibáñez, 2025).
text.formatted: Recent allostaticinteroceptive frameworks have emphasized the integration of biological regulation with social and environmental adversity <ref type="bibr" target="#b144">(Migeot and Ibáñez, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Consistently, multidimensional social exposome measures have been associated with cognitive, neuropsychiatric, and brain alterations in aging and neurodegenerative diseases (Migeot et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Consistently, multidimensional social exposome measures have been associated with cognitive, neuropsychiatric, and brain alterations in aging and neurodegenerative diseases <ref type="bibr">(Migeot et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These findings suggest that social conditions may influence both the emergence of dysfunction and the resources available to compensate for its consequences.

Together, middle adulthood may increase the opportunity for the three domains to become coupled, while the interplay between individual reserve and broader social and socioeconomic conditions may determine or moderate whether this coupling remains limited, involves two domains, or develops into a broader selfmaintaining regulatory failure.
We argue that another important source of variation is related to the main condition initially affected.

A similar idea has been proposed for cognitive impairment, physical frailty, and cardiovascular disease, where the condition that develops first may indicate the pathway driving pathological aging (Ijaz et al., 2024).
text.formatted: A similar idea has been proposed for cognitive impairment, physical frailty, and cardiovascular disease, where the condition that develops first may indicate the pathway driving pathological aging <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">(Ijaz et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: As mentioned above, researchers have identified at least three different profiles for LLD, which have been called depression executive dysfunction syndrome, vascular depression, and (immuno-)metabolic depression (Alexopoulos, 2019; Penninx et al., 2025).
text.formatted: As mentioned above, researchers have identified at least three different profiles for LLD, which have been called depression executive dysfunction syndrome, vascular depression, and (immuno-)metabolic depression <ref type="bibr">(Alexopoulos, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b167">Penninx et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These profiles are characterized by different symptomatology and might also be explained by different mechanisms and by different points of entry into the system.

When cardiometabolic burden is predominantly vascular, the resulting depressive syndrome tends to be dominated by psychomotor retardation, apathy, anhedonia, and executive dysfunction, a presentation that overlaps substantially with the depression-executive dysfunction syndrome and is consistent with frontostriatal disruption (Alexopoulos, 2019).
text.formatted: When cardiometabolic burden is predominantly vascular, the resulting depressive syndrome tends to be dominated by psychomotor retardation, apathy, anhedonia, and executive dysfunction, a presentation that overlaps substantially with the depression-executive dysfunction syndrome and is consistent with frontostriatal disruption <ref type="bibr">(Alexopoulos, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: When obesity, insulin resistance, and lowgrade inflammation predominate, the atypical, energy-related profile of immuno-metabolic depression is more likely (Penninx et al., 2025).
text.formatted: When obesity, insulin resistance, and lowgrade inflammation predominate, the atypical, energy-related profile of immuno-metabolic depression is more likely <ref type="bibr" target="#b167">(Penninx et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Genetic evidence is consistent with this distinction, since polygenic risk for stroke is associated only with later-onset depression, whereas polygenic risk for body mass index, coronary artery disease, and type 2 diabetes is associated with both early-and later-onset depression (Hagenaars et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Genetic evidence is consistent with this distinction, since polygenic risk for stroke is associated only with later-onset depression, whereas polygenic risk for body mass index, coronary artery disease, and type 2 diabetes is associated with both early-and later-onset depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Hagenaars et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: A comparable specificity may apply to the cognitive consequences of cardiometabolic dysfunction.

Hypertension has been associated with poorer executive function and processing speed (Pacholko and Iadecola, 2024), and moderates the association between cortisol regulation and processing speed (Pulopulos et al., 2016), whereas insulin resistance has been linked to lower glucose metabolism in medial temporal and prefrontal regions and to poorer working and short-term memory (Willette et al., 2015; Deery et al., 2024a), and brain insulin resistance has been proposed as a shared substrate of anhedonia and cognitive impairment in depression (Hamer et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Hypertension has been associated with poorer executive function and processing speed <ref type="bibr" target="#b163">(Pacholko and Iadecola, 2024)</ref>, and moderates the association between cortisol regulation and processing speed <ref type="bibr" target="#b180">(Pulopulos et al., 2016)</ref>, whereas insulin resistance has been linked to lower glucose metabolism in medial temporal and prefrontal regions and to poorer working and short-term memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b244">(Willette et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Deery et al., 2024a)</ref>, and brain insulin resistance has been proposed as a shared substrate of anhedonia and cognitive impairment in depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Hamer et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: When the first domain affected is cognitive, stress exposure interacting with factors that reduce neural resilience may favor a depression-executive dysfunction presentation.

For example, in healthy older adults, higher cortisol levels were associated with poorer declarative memory, particularly in carriers of the ApoE-ε4 allele, a major genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease, suggesting that this allele may confer vulnerability to the cognitive effects of HPA-axis dysregulation (Montoliu et al., 2018).
text.formatted: For example, in healthy older adults, higher cortisol levels were associated with poorer declarative memory, particularly in carriers of the ApoE-ε4 allele, a major genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease, suggesting that this allele may confer vulnerability to the cognitive effects of HPA-axis dysregulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b151">(Montoliu et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: In LLD, early onset is associated with a greater decline across all cognitive areas compared to late onset (Riddle et al., 2017), suggesting that if the psychological domain is affected initially and depression is recurrent, the cognitive effects tend to be more extensive.
text.formatted: In LLD, early onset is associated with a greater decline across all cognitive areas compared to late onset <ref type="bibr" target="#b193">(Riddle et al., 2017)</ref>, suggesting that if the psychological domain is affected initially and depression is recurrent, the cognitive effects tend to be more extensive.

text.text: Importantly, potentially traumatic experiences and particularly early-life adversity may further shape these entry points.

Adverse childhood experiences have been associated with enduring alterations in HPA-axis activity, prefrontal and hippocampal structure, and inflammation that may increase allostatic load and accelerate biological aging (Danese and McEwen, 2012).
text.formatted: Adverse childhood experiences have been associated with enduring alterations in HPA-axis activity, prefrontal and hippocampal structure, and inflammation that may increase allostatic load and accelerate biological aging <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Danese and McEwen, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Such early biological embedding could therefore accelerate the processes described here, influencing not only vulnerability within each domain but also how early, and how strongly, the three domains become coupled.
Moreover, the first clinically affected cognitive domain may not correspond to the earliest underlying biological disturbance.
Neurodegenerative and cerebrovascular processes can remain subclinical for extended periods, potentially influencing several domains before overt symptoms emerge, and involve compensatory mechanisms.

Identifying the initial point of entry into the proposed system may therefore require longitudinal biological and clinical characterization rather than reliance on the temporal order of symptom detection.
The same principle may help explain why some individuals develop one condition, others two, and others all three.
Longitudinal studies have linked the three domains in different sequences.

In the Rotterdam and Whitehall II cohorts, poorer cardiometabolic status predicted later depressive symptoms, which in turn predicted subsequent cognitive decline, alongside a direct cardiometabolic-cognitive association (Schmitz et al., 2018).
text.formatted: In the Rotterdam and Whitehall II cohorts, poorer cardiometabolic status predicted later depressive symptoms, which in turn predicted subsequent cognitive decline, alongside a direct cardiometabolic-cognitive association <ref type="bibr" target="#b203">(Schmitz et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: In the 1958 British birth cohort, affective symptoms accumulated across early and mid-adulthood were associated with midlife memory and verbal fluency through cardiometabolic risk (John et al., 2021).
text.formatted: In the 1958 British birth cohort, affective symptoms accumulated across early and mid-adulthood were associated with midlife memory and verbal fluency through cardiometabolic risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">(John et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, depressive symptoms were associated with steeper increases in glycaemic markers only among individuals with lower executive function in 1,257 African American and White, urban-dwelling adults from the Healthy Aging in Neighborhoods of Diversity across the Life Span (Khambaty et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Moreover, depressive symptoms were associated with steeper increases in glycaemic markers only among individuals with lower executive function in 1,257 African American and White, urban-dwelling adults from the Healthy Aging in Neighborhoods of Diversity across the Life Span <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">(Khambaty et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: These findings align with the idea that dysfunction may start at any node, with the first affected node shaping which others are recruited next.
Whether and how dysfunction spreads likely depends on the interaction between this initial perturbation and individual risk and protective factors.

To our knowledge, however, no study has examined, within the same cohort, the probability of developing none, one, two, or all three of these conditions as a function of the first affected domain and the risk and protective factors present.
Such studies will be necessary to determine whether the point of entry into the system predicts the combination of conditions an individual eventually develops.

In the previous sections, we have described how cognitive, cardiometabolic and psychological health problems associated with aging can be exacerbated and self-maintained by stress and the dysregulation of stress-related biological systems.
It is important to note that most cross-domain pathways reviewed here are supported by prospective observational evidence, whereas direct causal evidence remains limited.
Thus, the proposed feedback system should be understood as a testable mechanistic hypothesis rather than an established causal network.
Moreover, several gaps still need to be addressed to better understand how these conditions evolve with aging and the mechanisms behind their progression.
First, the directional pathways between domains should be examined with all three domains (cognitive, cardiometabolic, and psychological) measured, even when only one pathway is of primary interest.
We argue that the associations between the three conditions are not independent.

An association between cardiometabolic dysfunction and subsequent depressive symptoms may be direct, may be routed through declining cognitive control, or may be inflated because cognitive decline contributes to both.
A two-domain design cannot distinguish these possibilities, and the unmeasured domain then becomes an important and uninterpretable source of between-person variability.
Measuring the third domain is therefore valuable even when it is not the target, as it allows estimation of the pathway of interest while accounting for alternative routes.
Where repeated measures of all three domains are available, randomintercept cross-lagged panel models and related approaches can separate within-person change from stable between-person differences.

However, although such longitudinal models can help disentangle withinperson associations from stable between-person differences, they do not by themselves establish causal relationships, particularly in the presence of unmeasured time-varying confounding or measurement error.

Second, further studies testing the mechanisms proposed in the preceding sections, and whether their contribution changes with age, may offer valuable insights for developing effective preventive strategies.
In this context, age should not be treated as a confounder, as it is important to understand whether cross-domain coupling changes with age.

Age-moderated longitudinal models and time-varying network approaches, among other statistical approaches, could estimate whether psychological-tometabolic, metabolic-to-cognitive, and cognitive-to-psychological/metabolic pathways become progressively stronger across adulthood.

In such analyses, the parameter of primary interest is not an age difference in mean depression, metabolic syndrome, or cognitive performance, but the change in the magnitude of the prospective relationships among these domains.

Similarly, protective and compensatory resources should be modeled as moderators of the cross-domain pathways, as they may explain when individuals are at risk of developing relatively isolated dysfunction, coupling restricted to two domains, and a broader self-maintaining regulatory failure.

Such analyses should also consider interpersonal and socioeconomic conditions, including social support, education, occupational characteristics, and material resources, as potential determinants of stress exposure and moderators of cross-domain associations (Vanderhasselt et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Such analyses should also consider interpersonal and socioeconomic conditions, including social support, education, occupational characteristics, and material resources, as potential determinants of stress exposure and moderators of cross-domain associations <ref type="bibr" target="#b235">(Vanderhasselt et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This would help distinguish individual regulatory capacities from the social conditions that may facilitate or constrain their expression.
Third, given the large interindividual variability, more research is needed to understand specific health profiles, focusing on specific symptoms rather than general diagnoses.
As emphasized by Amad et al.

(2026) in the context of psychiatric disorders, a more precise characterization of symptom expression, including observable behavioral and physiological manifestations, may help identify clinically meaningful subgroups and provide a stronger foundation for investigating their underlying biological mechanisms.

For instance, patients sharing a diagnosis of depression may present opposite symptoms (e.g., insomnia vs. hypersomnia, weight loss vs. weight gain; Goldberg, 2011), and in a sample of more than 1,500 patients, the diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder were met through 170 different symptom combinations (Zimmerman et al., 2015).

text.text: In LLD, three profiles have been linked to executive, vascular, and (immuno-)metabolic dysfunction (Alexopoulos, 2019; Penninx et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In LLD, three profiles have been linked to executive, vascular, and (immuno-)metabolic dysfunction <ref type="bibr">(Alexopoulos, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b167">Penninx et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: We may also expect different symptomatology profiles in other conditions depending on the specific mechanisms involved.

Future studies should therefore test whether distinct symptom profiles, in the psychological as well as in the cardiometabolic and cognitive domains, are associated with distinct patterns of HPA-axis and ANS dysregulation and with different trajectories.
A more comprehensive cardiometabolic and neuropsychological characterization could also include relevant disease biomarkers and neuroimaging measures, when available.

Regarding cognitive decline, when combined with age-and education-adjusted norms and repeated assessments, such characterization would also allow testing whether stress-system dysregulation accelerates age-related cognitive change in the absence of overt pathology, increases vulnerability to (or hastens the expression of) neurodegenerative and cerebrovascular processes, or both.

Within this context, it is important to note that given the heterogeneity of cognitive assessments across studies, stronger associations involving executive functions could partly reflect differences in measurement sensitivity or the domains preferentially investigated.

Thus, cognitive assessment should extend beyond executive functions and global cognitive scores to encompass other cognitive domains, including episodic memory, language, visuo-constructive, and socio-affective functioning.
Fourth, studies should directly test whether dysfunction in the mechanisms linked to the three domains contributes to maintaining the dysregulation of the stress systems themselves.
Most of the research has focused on how dysregulation of the HPA axis and ANS predicts cognitive, cardiometabolic, and psychological health problems.
No research has investigated whether these conditions and their related mechanisms contribute to stress regulation and HPA axis and ANS profiles in aging.

Along this line, we argue that these conditions are linked to reduced context-sensitive regulation, leading to a weaker match between demand and response (i.e., activation that is excessive, insufficient, mistimed, or prolonged relative to the situation) rather than a simple elevation of any single marker.

Future studies could combine multidimensional allostatic load indices, integrating cardiovascular, metabolic, and neuroendocrine, and inflammatory markers, with measures of central allostatic-interoceptive processing, such as heartbeatevoked potentials and functional connectivity of the allostatic-interoceptive network.

Longitudinal assessments could help determine whether alterations in these physiological and neural systems precede, accompany, or follow cognitive and psychological changes, including in populations at risk of neurodegenerative disease (Birba et al., 2022; Marin-Díaz et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Longitudinal assessments could help determine whether alterations in these physiological and neural systems precede, accompany, or follow cognitive and psychological changes, including in populations at risk of neurodegenerative disease <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Birba et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b128">Marin-Díaz et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Including measures of biological aging would further allow testing whether stronger coupling among the three domains, and the stress-system dysregulation that sustains it, predicts accelerated biological aging.
Such designs should account for the fact that different organs and systems may age at different rates (Zhang, 2023).
text.formatted: Such designs should account for the fact that different organs and systems may age at different rates <ref type="bibr" target="#b253">(Zhang, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Fifth, prevention and intervention studies should target the shared regulatory mechanisms.
We predict that interventions targeting shared regulatory mechanisms should produce effects across more than one condition.

Small nonrandomized studies already point to such cross-domain effects, with cognitive improvement after treating cardiac dysfunction (e.g., aortic valve replacement or cardiac resynchronization therapy; van Nieuwkerk et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Small nonrandomized studies already point to such cross-domain effects, with cognitive improvement after treating cardiac dysfunction (e.g., aortic valve replacement or cardiac resynchronization therapy; <ref type="bibr" target="#b236">van Nieuwkerk et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Bottom-up approaches, acting on the peripheral and afferent side of the neurovisceral circuit, and top-down approaches, acting on its prefrontal node, may be particularly important to change the mechanisms described above.

Exercise and physical activity are obvious examples because they can simultaneously improve cardiometabolic function, cognitive function, and psychological well-being, including in middle-aged and older populations, although the exact mechanisms and the types of patients who benefit most are still not well understood (Penedo and Dahn, 2005; Pérez-López et al., 2017; Van Damme et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Exercise and physical activity are obvious examples because they can simultaneously improve cardiometabolic function, cognitive function, and psychological well-being, including in middle-aged and older populations, although the exact mechanisms and the types of patients who benefit most are still not well understood <ref type="bibr" target="#b166">(Penedo and Dahn, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b168">Pérez-López et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b231">Van Damme et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, voluntary slow-paced breathing, considered both a bottom-up and topdown approach, reliably increases vagally mediated HRV both acutely and following repeated practice (Laborde et al., 2022; Li et al., 2024b).

text.text: Non-invasive prefrontal stimulation offers another mechanistically informative approach, as meta-analytic evidence indicates that cortical stimulation can alter heart rate, HRV, and stress-induced cortisol regulation, supporting the causal involvement of cortical systems in HPA axis and autonomic regulation (Pulopulos et al., 2020a; Schmaußer et al., 2022).

text.text: Transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation offers another route to the afferent pathways, as it has been shown to affect LC activity and interoception (Roy and Vanderhasselt, 2026).
text.formatted: Transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation offers another route to the afferent pathways, as it has been shown to affect LC activity and interoception <ref type="bibr" target="#b194">(Roy and Vanderhasselt, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, middle-aged adults could represent a particularly important preventive window, when dysfunction is emerging but compensatory neural and physiological mechanisms remain available.

This possibility is consistent with both the revised Scaffolding Theory of Aging and Cognition and recent evidence that midlife is a turning point when metabolic plasticity of brain networks begins to decline (Reuter-Lorenz and Park, 2014; Antal et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This possibility is consistent with both the revised Scaffolding Theory of Aging and Cognition and recent evidence that midlife is a turning point when metabolic plasticity of brain networks begins to decline <ref type="bibr" target="#b189">(Reuter-Lorenz and Park, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Antal et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond these individual-level approaches, interventions targeting interpersonal processes and social support could also be investigated as potential means of modifying stressrelated feedback mechanisms (Vanderhasselt et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Beyond these individual-level approaches, interventions targeting interpersonal processes and social support could also be investigated as potential means of modifying stressrelated feedback mechanisms <ref type="bibr" target="#b235">(Vanderhasselt et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Such studies could examine whether improvements in relationship quality, interpersonal emotion regulation, or psychological support are accompanied by changes in psychological and physiological stress regulation.

Crucially, future intervention studies should not simply determine whether these approaches improve one isolated outcome, but whether improvements in vagal regulation, prefrontal functioning, or HPA and adrenergic flexibility explain improvements across domains.
Such a design would directly test whether modifying the shared regulatory substrate changes the coupling between the three nodes.

Conversely, if an intervention substantially improved one domain but repeatedly failed to influence the others or their prospective coupling, this would constitute evidence against the stronger form of the selfmaintaining-system hypothesis.

Importantly, such studies should also assess whether changes in cognitive and physiological regulation translate into clinically meaningful improvements in everyday functioning and psychological well-being.
Depression and anxiety, cognitive decline, and cardiometabolic dysfunction are common in older adults and have been independently linked to dysregulation of the HPA axis and ANS.

In this review, we suggest that what appears epidemiologically as comorbidity among stress-related health problems in late adulthood may partly stem from a failure of a shared regulatory system that maintains them.
We extend the discussion from mere comorbidity to view depression and anxiety, cognitive decline, and cardiometabolic dysfunction as interconnected components of a potentially reinforcing system.
Existing evidence indicates directional pathways connecting these health issues.

Key stress-regulation mechanisms may underlie how changes in one area affect others, potentially influencing stress-regulation systems during aging and contributing to ongoing HPA axis and ANS dysregulation.

Middle adulthood emerges as a critical period when the impact of stress and allostatic load on health can be seen not only as cumulative effects of stress, but also as the progressive manifestation of a regulatory system in which psychological, cognitive, and cardiometabolic issues increasingly sustain each other.
